analysis.one_liner: Lets the Energy Department block major EPA energy rules and bars counting carbon's social costs.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it was referred to a House subcommittee in November 2015 and never received a vote, markup, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to submit detailed cost, price, and job-impact reports before finalizing any energy-related rule estimated to cost over $100 million [S2]. It would then let the Department of Energy block the rule entirely if DOE determined it would cause "significant adverse effects to the economy" [S2][S3]. It also banned the EPA from using the social cost of carbon — the government's standard tool for valuing the damages from carbon pollution — in any cost-benefit analysis of major energy rules unless Congress passed a law authorizing it [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to a House subcommittee and never advanced [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coal, oil, and gas producers and other large polluters would benefit most, since the bill gives another agency a veto over EPA climate and pollution rules and strips the main way those rules' benefits are measured [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fossil fuel producers facing EPA rules

how_it_helps.text: Before finalizing any energy rule costing over $100 million, the EPA would have to report its total costs, estimated energy-price increases for consumers, and projected job losses to Congress and the Energy Department [S2][S3].

The Department of Energy could refuse to allow the rule to be finalized if it determined the rule would cause significant adverse effects to the economy — a veto power over EPA rulemaking that does not exist in current law [S2][S3].

The bill would prohibit the EPA from using the social cost of carbon in cost-benefit analyses of major energy rules unless a new federal law authorized it, making large climate rules much harder to justify economically [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the health and climate costs of weakened air-pollution and carbon rules — the harms the bill makes harder for the EPA to account for — while energy producers avoid compliance costs [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to pollution and climate damage

drawbacks.text: Removing the social cost of carbon would erase the government's only standardized measure of climate damages — estimated at roughly tens of dollars per ton of carbon dioxide in the 2013 technical document the bill targets — which would make the benefits of carbon rules disappear on paper [S2][S3].

Handing the Department of Energy a veto over EPA rules would slow or kill pollution standards even where the EPA found benefits exceeded costs, and supporters would argue it instead adds a needed second look at rules that raise energy prices for households and manufacturers — a cost an honest opponent should weigh [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is framed as consumer protection, but its binding provisions do not lower anyone's energy bill; they make it harder for the EPA to finalize pollution and climate rules by adding a second agency's veto and discarding the standard measure of climate benefits [S2][S3]. Whatever value the added reporting has, the practical effect is to shield energy producers from regulation, with the costs landing on the public as pollution and climate damage [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee from November 2015 until Congress ended in January 2017, never getting a markup or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Fleming (R-LA) introduced the bill on November 17, 2015, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and three days later to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power [S5].
No further action was recorded for the rest of the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, but the EPA's authority to write energy and climate rules — including its use of the social cost of carbon — was left intact, so the fossil fuel producers the bill would have shielded gained nothing but lost nothing either; the public avoided a new obstacle to pollution rules.

for.name: John Fleming
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it drew no cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Energy and Power and took no further action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no record exists of how members would have split; the sponsor was a Republican in a Republican-controlled Congress.

industries.note: If passed, the bill would have given these producers a veto-protected path around EPA pollution and climate rules costing over $100 million, and would have stripped the social cost of carbon that measures the harm their emissions cause [S2][S3]. The industry's gain would come at the public's expense in avoided regulation [S2][S3].

Utilities burning fossil fuels would face fewer mandated emissions cuts if EPA rules were blocked, but the bill's own analysis requirements target rising electricity prices for consumers, including from reliance on costlier fuels [S2][S3]. Its main effect on utilities would be relief from new regulation [S2][S3].
